rv.q: Lea Michele is delivering a tour de force for the ages.

Any lingering thoughts in audience members’ minds about the show’s bumpy beginnings are likely to melt away as soon as Ms. Michele takes the stage, instantly galvanizing a previously lackluster production into radiant life.

rv.cn: Broadway Glee: Dazzling Lea Michele Delivers in Funny Girl
rv.q: But love it or hate it, the end result of the mess is undeniable: Michele delivered, and Funny Girl has leveled up.
But with Feldstein firmly steering the ship, “Funny Girl” is a breezy and joyful ride.
But she never quite makes the material soar, and this is a rickety vehicle that needs a supernova to put gas in its tank.
But the show rests and falls on Feldstein, who must posses as Brice both a grand confidence — “I’m the greatest star” — and an insecurity (“You mean it?”).
Feldstein can only do so much as a Broadway star with what she has to offer at this point.
Feldstein's Fanny is more sweet than sassy, more earnest than manic, which makes for a perfectly pleasant performance that doesn't quite capture the character's supposed star quality.
But this is a musical, one with some full-tilt belting, and her singing just isn’t up to par.
But you know a production of Funny Girl hasn't clicked when you leave thinking, Well, at least it was pretty.
It seems brutal to place a woman in such an exposed position, where a whole Broadway production rests on notes she can’t sustain.
Rather than incandescent, though, Feldstein’s star turn is an earthbound affair, best when she’s executing the comedy aspect of musical comedy, and less compelling at the music part.
And without a stupendous Fanny to thrill and distract, the musical’s manifold faults become painfully evident.
Feldstein's big-note numbers land well, especially 'I'm the Greatest Star' and 'Don't Rain on My Parade.'
This sorely lacking new production rains on the old musical’s parade.
But the reason to see “Funny Girl” is Michele as she secures her place in Broadway history.
Funny Girl is a brilliant work, and with Feldstein, radiates pure theatrical joy.
But even without all the added contextual layers, Michele stands alone as a singular Broadway performer, one who can pack a house and command a crowd and also hit all the right notes and laughs.
With her at the center, it feels impossible to rain on the parade.
As of this revival, those notes might have exiting customers happily thinking “Beanie Feldstein, Beanie Feldstein.”
Right now, with Lea Michele at the helm, Funny Girl is landing the big moments.
While Ms. Feldstein may not be the greatest star one could ever imagine to carry “Funny Girl,” she proves herself most worthy of this company and these surroundings.
More than that, it's hard to escape the feeling that Feldstein, for all her fourth-wall winks and bright enthusiasm, is fundamentally miscast.

"Beanie Feldstein is, it turns out, a perfectly fine choice for this 'Funny Girl,' which is not to say she’s perfect, but rather that she’s on equal footing with a just-above-average musical that has always been dominated by several excellent songs and a legendary breakout performance that lifted the show – and its plodding 1968 movie adaptation...
Beanie Feldstein is a charming and accomplished performer, but she's not quite the powerhouse vocalist this role demands.
The answer to both questions is, ultimately, no.
The answer, in short, is neither — a dissatisfying conclusion for those who have eagerly anticipated either fireworks or flames.
Consequently, her star turn never quite lifts off the stage.
Sometimes it is time to call a bluff. I'm calling it.
Sadly like a lot in Funny Girl 2022—rings hollow.
It’s a witless cliché, and a counterproductive one.
I have no doubt that Funny Girl will experience a lengthy extended run—to return again to see either Michele or her understudy, Julie Benko, would truly be a treat.

With Isobel Lennart's book reworked some by Harvey Fierstein, Funny Girl is at its best when the comedy is front and center, and Feldstein is a first-rate comedian who knows how to mine a scene for every laugh.
Though she gives it her very best, she does not make it over the finish line in good shape.
Future discussions of this Funny Girl will be unable to ignore the elephant in the room: would its fate have been seriously altered by a different casting decision?
But the producers would have been better off spending more time casting the lead.
The totality of her performance is a fascinating instance of delusional adequacy.
Feldstein tries, and comes nowhere close to succeeding, but reveals something deeper: take Barbra away, and Funny Girl is not a good musical.
